title: Jimmy Cricket: clean comedy that charmed generations
seoTitle: Jimmy Cricket: clean comedy that charmed generations
subtitle: Meet the comedian who avoided profanity and earned a papal honor
excerpt: Jimmy Cricket, stage name of James Joseph Mulgrew, died at 80 on August 4, 2026. His career, marked by non-vulgar humor, went beyond.
author: Daniele Morais
contentHtml:
On August 4, 2026, Jimmy Cricket died at the age of 80. Known for the catchphrase “And there’s more!”, the comedian left a legacy of light, non-vulgar entertainment.

The early years in holiday camps

James Joseph Mulgrew, a native of Cookstown, Northern Ireland, began performing in British holiday camps in the 1960s, working at the Butlin’s and Pontins establishments. It was there that he adopted the stage name Jimmy Cricket, inspired by delicate euphemisms for the exclamation “Jesus Christ!”.

Peak on television and radio

Between 1985 and 1988, the artist hosted the ITV programme “And There’s More”, airing 24 episodes of sketches, songs, and stand-up. The regular cast included Nicholas Smith and Joan Sims, while guests such as Hazel O’Connor and Rory Bremner made special appearances. In 1990, BBC Radio 2 launched the series “Jimmy’s Cricket Team”, reinforcing his presence in audio media.

The non-vulgar comedic style

Jimmy Cricket appeared in short formal trousers, funny hats and rubber boots (Wellingtons) worn on the wrong feet, a look that led some to think he was a children’s entertainer. However, his target audience was adults, offering entertainment classified as a “family entertainer”: no obscenities, no profanity, and only a few songs, in which his Irish accent allowed rhymes such as “faffing” with “laughing”. The routines contained references to “Mammy” letters and “Irish logic”, reflections of his Catholic upbringing in the 1950s.

Papal recognition and legacy

In 2015, Pope Francis awarded Jimmy Cricket the papal knighthood, the highest Catholic honour, recognizing his charitable work. The same title had been granted to compatriot Frank Carson by Pope John Paul II, establishing a pattern among comedians of the same generation.

His stance during the Northern Ireland conflict

During the period known as the Troubles, marked by violence in Northern Ireland, the comedian kept a distance from sectarian issues, focusing on an audience that rarely became holiday-camp customers. This stance prevented him from becoming a target of prejudice, although his Irish pronunciation was often the subject of imitation by other performers.

With information from The Guardian.
